strengths: Principled axiomatic formulation: The paper clearly sets up axioms for diffusion operators on general discrete domains (M-symmetry, mass conservation/constant preservation, non-negativity, and spectral damping), providing a unified perspective connecting Laplacians, message-passing, and kernel smoothing.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The authors provide complete proofs showing that symmetric Sinkhorn scaling yields a valid diffusion operator (Theorem 4.4), establish stability under measure refinement for fixed bandwidth (Theorem 4.5), and derive a tight relative error bound under mass perturbations (Proposition 4.6).

High computational efficiency and GPU friendliness: Reformulating diffusion via symmetric Sinkhorn normalization eliminates the need for expensive mesh factorizations or truncated Laplacian eigendecompositions. With only 5-10 iterations required, it scales seamlessly to large point sets via KeOps and attention formulations.

Broad and versatile experimental validation: The framework is convincingly evaluated across diverse modalities (triangle/tetrahedral meshes, point clouds, voxel grids, and Gaussian mixtures) and tasks, including spectral analysis, regularized gradient flows, LDDMM geodesic deformation, and deep geometric learning (Q-DiffNet).
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical novelty relative to prior optimal transport and manifold learning works: The mathematical machinery heavily builds on existing results in symmetric matrix scaling (Knight et al., 2014) and regularized OT (Feydy et al., 2019). While the focus on fixed bandwidth and geometry processing axioms is well-motivated, the core algorithmic mechanism is essentially an application of existing symmetric Sinkhorn scaling.

Residual reliance on mesh structures in deep learning evaluation: In the main shape matching experiment (Table 2), the strongest variant of Q-DiffNet still relies on mesh-derived WKS descriptors and ground-truth functional map baselines. When evaluating fully unstructured setups (Q-DiffNet with Q-FM or raw XYZ coordinates in Table 4), performance drops noticeably and is roughly on par with existing point cloud baselines.

Sensitivity to mass and bandwidth estimation: While Proposition 4.6 bounds error amplification under mass perturbation, computing the mass matrix $M$ and selecting bandwidth $\sigma$ on complex, non-uniformly sampled irregular geometries still requires empirical heuristics (such as local KDE).

strengths: Principled and unifying theoretical framework: The paper provides a clean axiomatic formulation connecting smoothing, Laplace-like operators, and diffusion operators across diverse geometric modalities (graphs, point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, and voxel grids). It guarantees key physical and structural invariants (mass conservation, M-symmetry, entrywise positivity, and spectral boundedness in [0, 1]).

Focus on practical, fixed-bandwidth stability: Unlike standard manifold learning literature (e.g., Wormell & Reich 2021, Cheng & Landa 2024) that focuses on the asymptotic joint limit (N -> inf, sigma -> 0), this work addresses the fixed-scale regime actually used in geometry processing. The proofs of uniform convergence under refinement (Theorem 4.5) and relative stability under mass perturbations (Proposition 4.6) are mathematically rigorous and practically meaningful.

Computational elegance and GPU friendliness: The symmetric Sinkhorn normalization is matrix-free, requires only a few matrix-vector products (converging in 5-10 iterations), avoids expensive sparse matrix factorizations or truncated eigendecompositions, and maps cleanly to fast modern routines (KeOps, attention-style implementations).

Diverse and convincing validation: The proposed operator is validated across multiple downstream tasks, including consistent spectral analysis across 4 distinct shape modalities (Figure 3), regularizing gradient flows (Figure 4), preventing contraction/expansion degeneracies in Hamiltonian geodesic shooting / LDDMM (Figure 5), and competitive performance when integrated into a deep shape-correspondence pipeline (Q-DiffNet in ULRSSM).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: The core mathematical mechanism—symmetric Sinkhorn scaling—is directly imported from the numerical linear algebra and optimal transport literature (Knight et al., 2014; Feydy et al., 2019). The primary novelty lies in the geometric interpretation and its application to unstructured geometric processing rather than an entirely new algorithm.

Dependence on the mass matrix discretization: While Proposition 4.6 bounds the sensitivity to mass perturbations, the operator's geometric fidelity fundamentally relies on having a reasonable mass matrix M. In severely non-uniform, noisy, or sparse point clouds, mass estimation remains a non-trivial heuristic (e.g., relying on KDE or Voronoi cells).

Empirical gains in deep learning are mixed: In the non-rigid shape correspondence experiments (Table 2), Q-DiffNet performs comparably to existing point-based baselines on FAUST (2.1 vs 2.3) and SCAPE (2.4 vs 2.4), though it shows a significant advantage on SHREC19 (3.5 vs 5.1). Furthermore, Table 2 relies on mesh-derived WKS descriptors to isolate the diffusion operator's impact; when switching to raw XYZ coordinates (Table 4), performance drops substantially across all models.

Lack of infinitesimal Laplacian convergence guarantees: As noted in the limitations, while Q acts as a well-behaved diffusion surrogate at scale sigma > 0, the paper does not prove asymptotic convergence of (I - Q) / sigma^2 to the true continuous Laplace-Beltrami operator on irregular discrete structures.

strengths: Principled and elegant conceptual framework: The paper introduces a clear axiomatic characterization of diffusion operators on discrete domains (mass preservation, symmetry w.r.t. a mass-weighted inner product, positivity, and spectrum in [0, 1]) and resolves the trade-off between row-stochasticity and symmetry via symmetric Sinkhorn normalization.

Solid theoretical support: The authors provide rigorous proofs connecting symmetric Sinkhorn scaling to entropy-regularized optimal transport (Theorem 4.4), prove stability under sampling refinement for fixed bandwidth kernels (Theorem 4.5), and derive an informative first-order stability bound w.r.t. mass matrix perturbations (Proposition 4.6).

Versatility across data modalities: The proposed approach is demonstrated across triangle/tetrahedral meshes, point clouds, Gaussian mixture models, and voxel grids, showing consistent spectral properties without requiring explicit manifold connectivity.

Strong practical efficiency and GPU suitability: By avoiding sparse linear solves or factorizations (such as implicit Euler or Cholesky) and formulating the operation via symmetric Sinkhorn iterations, the method enables fast GPU kernel operations compatible with KeOps and attention mechanisms.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated thoroughly across multiple tasks, including spectral shape analysis, particle gradient flow stabilization, LDDMM shape geodesic shooting, and learning-based non-rigid shape correspondence (Q-DiffNet in ULRSSM).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is moderate: Symmetric Sinkhorn scaling (Knight et al., 2014) and its ties to entropy-regularized OT (Feydy et al., 2019) and bi-stochastic graph Laplacians (Marshall & Coifman 2019; Wormell & Reich 2021; Cheng & Landa 2024) are well established. While the fixed-scale geometry processing viewpoint and multi-modal application are valuable, the mathematical machinery is largely synthesized from existing literature.

Residual reliance on mesh structures in the deep learning experiments: In Table 2, Q-DiffNet uses ground-truth mesh-derived WKS descriptors and mesh-based functional map eigenvectors to isolate feature extraction. The fully mesh-free variant (Q-FM) shows noticeable performance drops (e.g., 2.5 vs 1.6 on FAUST, 3.1 vs 2.1 on SCAPE), and the raw XYZ coordinate baseline in Table 4 degrades significantly across all methods.

Sensitivity to bandwidth parameter: As indicated in the appendix (Figure 10), eigenspaces degrade outside the range [0.5, 2.0] around the chosen scale sigma_0, making scale selection an important hyperparameter in practice.

Minor presentation issues: In Section 4 (Page 5), the text repeatedly refers to 'Theorem 4.1' and 'Theorem 4.3' when referring to Definition 4.1 and Definition 4.3. There is also a typo on Page 9 ('botter than with point-based baselines').

strengths: Principled and elegant formulation: The paper formalizes an axiomatic framework for diffusion operators on arbitrary discrete geometric representations (point clouds, voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures, and graphs) and uses symmetric Sinkhorn scaling to obtain operators that jointly satisfy symmetry with respect to a mass metric, constant preservation (mass conservation), damping, and positivity.

Solid theoretical backing: The connection to entropy-regularized optimal transport is mathematically clear and well-leveraged. Theorem 4.1 proves normalization and spectral damping in $[0, 1]$, and Theorem 4.2 establishes weak convergence of the normalized discrete operators to a well-defined continuous limit operator under fixed kernel scale.

Broad applicability and versatility: The proposed construction is validated across diverse tasks, including multi-modal spectral shape analysis (matching mesh FEM spectra across points, voxels, and GMMs), gradient flow preconditioning for particle optimization, LDDMM geodesic shooting in computational anatomy, and deep learning for non-rigid shape correspondence (Q-DiffNet).

High computational efficiency and practicality: The symmetric Sinkhorn scaling requires only 5–10 matrix-vector multiplications, does not require matrix factorizations or mesh connectivity, and can be easily implemented with GPU-accelerated symbolic matrix / attention libraries like KeOps and FlashAttention.
weaknesses: Lack of convergence analysis in the infinitesimal kernel bandwidth regime ($\sigma \to 0$): As the authors acknowledge, Theorem 4.2 establishes convergence for fixed $\sigma$ as sample resolution grows, but does not prove spectral or operator convergence to the true continuous Laplace–Beltrami operator as bandwidth $\sigma \to 0$.

Dependencies in the deep shape matching setup: In the point feature learning experiment (Section 6, Table/Figure 6), the input WKS features are still precomputed from the ground-truth mesh Laplacian to isolate the operator's impact. While understandable for fair comparison, evaluating fully mesh-free scenarios from raw coordinates or purely point-derived descriptors across all baselines would more conclusively demonstrate standalone point cloud performance.

strengths: Principled and clear formulation: The paper clearly sets up the axiomatic requirements for discrete diffusion operators (mass-weighted symmetry, constant preservation, spectral damping, and entrywise positivity) and shows how symmetric Sinkhorn scaling satisfies these properties simultaneously.

Unification across unstructured modalities: The proposed approach provides a unified mechanism to define heat-like diffusion across diverse geometric representations—including unstructured point clouds, sparse voxel grids, and Gaussian mixtures—without requiring mesh connectivity or local manifold reconstruction.

Computational feasibility: The algorithm requires only 5–10 iterations of matrix-vector products and integrates well with GPU-accelerated symbolic matrix tools (such as KeOps) and fast attention mechanisms, avoiding the costly linear solves or Cholesky factorizations typical of implicit Euler heat diffusion.

Diverse proof-of-concept experiments: The framework is demonstrated on several distinct downstream applications, ranging from spectral shape analysis and particle gradient flows to diffeomorphic shape interpolation (LDDMM) and deep learning for non-rigid shape matching (Q-DiffNet).
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical novelty: Symmetrized Sinkhorn scaling and its link to graph Laplacians and diffusion maps have been studied previously in the optimal transport and manifold learning literature (e.g., Knight et al., 2014; Feydy et al., 2019; Marshall & Coifman, 2019; Cheng & Landa, 2024). Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 are largely adaptations of existing entropy-regularized OT convergence results rather than entirely new mathematical machinery.

Lack of convergence to the continuous Laplace–Beltrami operator: The convergence result (Theorem 4.2) holds for a fixed kernel bandwidth $\sigma$ as sample size increases, but does not establish convergence to the true Laplace–Beltrami operator as $\sigma \to 0$. Consequently, the operator acts as a normalized integral operator rather than a true differential operator.

Compromises and dependencies in the deep learning benchmark: In the shape correspondence experiment (Section 6 and Appendix H), Q-DiffNet still relies on WKS descriptors computed from the ground-truth mesh Laplacian to maintain competitive accuracy. When evaluating the fully autonomous pipeline using eigenvectors derived directly from the normalized operator (Q-DiffNet QFM), performance degrades notably on FAUST (2.5 vs 1.6) and SCAPE (3.1 vs 2.1).

Primarily qualitative evaluation on downstream geometric tasks: The particle gradient flow and LDDMM interpolation tasks (Figures 4 and 5) are evaluated purely through visual examples rather than standardized quantitative metrics against competing non-rigid registration or generative trajectory baselines.

strengths: Principled and unified framework: The paper provides an elegant algebraic and optimal transport formulation for constructing mass-preserving, self-adjoint diffusion operators from arbitrary symmetric similarity matrices across diverse data modalities (point clouds, sparse voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures, graphs).

Sound theoretical grounding: The discrete and continuous axioms for Laplace-like and diffusion operators are clearly formalized, and rigorous proofs are supplied connecting symmetric Sinkhorn scaling to spectrum damping (eigenvalues in [0, 1]), mass conservation, and continuous convergence under weak measure convergence.

Broad and versatile empirical evaluation: The proposed operator is successfully showcased across a diverse spectrum of tasks, including spectral shape analysis, preconditioning particle gradient flows, geodesic interpolation in LDDMM shape spaces, and 3D shape correspondence in deep learning.

Efficient and GPU-friendly formulation: The method avoids explicit matrix inversion, mesh triangulations, or expensive eigendecompositions, and connects naturally to KeOps and fast attention mechanisms.
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical delta over prior Sinkhorn/bi-stochastic literature: Symmetric Sinkhorn scaling and bi-stochastic normalization have been studied extensively in optimal transport (e.g., Feydy et al., 2019) and manifold learning (e.g., Marshall & Coifman, 2019; Cheng & Landa, 2024). While the mass-weighted formulation and discrete differential geometry interpretation are neat, the core algorithmic machinery is largely an adaptation of established techniques.

Reliance on mesh-derived quantities in the point feature learning experiments: As clarified in Appendix H, the primary Q-DiffNet evaluation utilizes WKS descriptors and training loss functional maps computed from ground-truth mesh Laplacians. While Q-DiffNet (QFM) evaluates a mesh-free functional map variant, the reliance on mesh-derived descriptors somewhat weakens the claim of fully mesh-independent learning.

Absence of quantitative runtime and memory benchmarks: The paper frequently emphasizes efficiency and GPU friendliness, but does not provide wall-clock timings or peak memory comparisons against standard DiffusionNet or sparse Cholesky/implicit Euler baselines on large-scale point clouds or voxel grids.

Fixed-scale vs. infinitesimal convergence: Theorem 4.2 holds for a fixed kernel bandwidth $\sigma > 0$ as sample resolution increases, rather than establishing spectral convergence to the true manifold Laplace–Beltrami operator as $\sigma \to 0$. Consequently, the operator acts as a mollified/kernel diffusion rather than a strictly consistent discretization of the Riemannian Laplacian.
